title: Septic shock from a urinary source

card.complaint: Fever, confusion and low blood pressure

triage.note: Brought by her son. Two days of burning when passing urine and fever; since this morning she is confused and has passed very little urine. Type 2 diabetes.

speech.impairedText: (Muddled and drowsy. She can’t give a clear answer. Ask her son.)

appearance.text: Warmer and more alert. Talking sensibly.
Flushed, a little confused but answering questions.
Hot, flushed and confused. Mottled knees.
Drowsy, cold and mottled peripheries, barely responding.

history.q: Ask her son what has happened
history.a: Two days ago she said it burned when she passed urine and she had a fever. This morning she didn’t know where she was and she’s hardly passed any urine.
Penicillin: she came out in an itchy rash years ago. Nothing worse than that.
Diabetes and blood pressure. She had a kidney infection two years ago.

history.q: Any burning or pain passing urine, or loin pain?
history.a: It burns… and my back hurts on the right.

history.q: Any cough, diarrhoea, headache or rash?

history.a: Hot… so tired. Where am I?

variants.text: Better, thank you. I’m in hospital, aren’t I?

exam.label: Circulation
exam.text: Bounding then thready pulse, capillary refill 4 s, mottling over the knees.

exam.label: Abdomen & loins
exam.text: Suprapubic tenderness and right renal-angle tenderness. No peritonism.

exam.label: Neurological
exam.text: GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6). No neck stiffness. No focal deficit.

variants.text: GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5). No neck stiffness.

exam.label: Skin
exam.text: No rash. No cellulitis. No pressure sores.

investigations.label: Venous gas with lactate
investigations.text: pH 7.29, HCO₃⁻ 16 mmol/L, lactate 4.6 mmol/L, glucose 13.2 mmol/L (238 mg/dL).

investigations.label: Urine dipstick
investigations.text: Leucocytes +++, nitrites positive, blood ++. Sample sent for culture.

investigations.label: Blood cultures (2 sets)
investigations.text: Two sets taken before antibiotics. Gram-negative bacilli will be reported at 18 h.

investigations.label: FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, coagulation
investigations.text: WCC 21.4 ×10⁹/L, CRP 286 mg/L, creatinine 212 µmol/L (2.4 mg/dL) (baseline 90), urea 18 mmol/L, bilirubin normal, platelets 132 ×10⁹/L, INR 1.3.

investigations.label: Ultrasound kidneys & bladder
investigations.text: Swollen right kidney. No hydronephrosis or stone: no obstruction needing drainage.

interventions.label: Call senior / critical-care outreach
interventions.say: Nurse: “Outreach team are on their way.”

interventions.label: Crystalloid 500 mL IV bolus
interventions.detail: Balanced crystalloid over 15 min; reassess after each

interventions.label: Urinary catheter, hourly urine output
interventions.say: Nurse: “Catheter in: 20 mL of dark, cloudy urine.”

interventions.label: Noradrenaline infusion
interventions.detail: Target MAP ≥ 65 mmHg; peripheral line acceptable short-term
interventions.feedback: A vasopressor is indicated when MAP stays below 65 mmHg despite fluids. Starting it through a good peripheral cannula while central access is arranged is acceptable.

interventions.label: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV
interventions.feedback: With a non-severe (rash-only) penicillin allergy, third-generation cephalosporins are generally acceptable. Follow your local antimicrobial policy.

interventions.label: Gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV (single dose)
interventions.feedback: A single dose is often used for urosepsis, but check renal function and follow local policy: this patient has an acute kidney injury.

interventions.label: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV

harm.why: Piperacillin–tazobactam is a penicillin. The patient has a documented penicillin allergy.

interventions.say: Nurse: “She’s coming out in hives on her arms…”

harm.why: Oral amoxicillin is inadequate for septic shock and she is penicillin-allergic.

interventions.label: Withhold metformin and ramipril
interventions.say: Nurse: “I’ve marked them as held on the chart.”

diagnoses.label: Septic shock from a urinary source (pyelonephritis)
Hypovolaemic shock from a GI bleed

dispositions.label: Admit to a general medical ward

critical.label: IV antibiotics within 1 hour
critical.why: In septic shock give effective antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 hour of recognition. Each hour of delay increases mortality.

critical.label: Fluid resuscitation started
critical.why: Hypotension and a lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L need rapid crystalloid (about 30 mL/kg in the first 3 hours), reassessed after each bolus.

critical.label: Lactate measured
critical.why: Lactate identifies shock and guides resuscitation.

critical.label: Monitoring attached
critical.why: Continuous observations are needed in shock.

recommended.label: At least 1.5 L crystalloid (≈ 30 mL/kg for 60 kg)
Looked for the source (urine dip / loin exam)

penalties.why: Antibiotics were given before blood cultures. Take cultures first when this causes no delay.
Antibiotics were given before blood cultures. Take cultures first when this causes no delay.

teaching: Septic shock: sepsis with vasopressors needed to keep MAP ≥ 65 mmHg and lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids. Hypotension with lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L is managed as shock from the start.

Hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, take blood cultures, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, start crystalloid (about 30 mL/kg for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4), and start a vasopressor if MAP stays below 65 mmHg.
Take cultures before antibiotics, but never delay antibiotics to do so.
Always check allergies. A rash-only penicillin allergy does not usually rule out cephalosporins or carbapenems; an anaphylactic one needs a different plan.
Look for a source that needs control (obstructed kidney, abscess, infected line). An obstructed infected kidney needs urgent drainage.
Monitor urine output with a catheter and withhold nephrotoxic drugs and metformin in acute kidney injury.
Escalate early to critical care when hypotension persists after fluids.
references: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: international guidelines for management of sepsis and septic shock 2021.
NICE NG51. Suspected sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management (updated 2024).
